title: OPERATION SLOW BURN
skeleton: a boarding element must cut a docked raider JumpShip out of a shared neutral recharge anchorage and fly it off intact before its drive finishes spinning up, where the prize must leave under power undamaged and the anchorage's enforced neutrality voids the contract the instant the unit's guns speak inside the bond
inspiration: the cutting-out of HMS Hermione from Puerto Cabello harbour, 1799
situation:
The {DISTRICT} anchorage is the only commercial recharge station for four jumps in any direction. Since the Blackout, it has survived by being the one place in the region where nobody shoots. Privateers, honest haulers, and the odd House courier all wait in the same charging queue under a station bond. The operators enforce that bond with the only weapon that works out here: a blacklist that follows a ship to every port still trading. Your unit holds a quiet retainer from {EMPLOYER} for a job the bond was never meant to allow.

Docked at the outer ring is the Karyatid, a Merchant-class JumpShip. A band called the Ash Company captured her eighteen months ago and has used her as a mobile raid base ever since. She is here for the reason everyone is here: to recharge. {EMPLOYER}, through {NPC:employer-contact}, wants her back intact — not sunk, not burned, but flown out from under her crew and handed over. Why is {EMPLOYER}'s business. Your unit was told only that the hull is worth more than the contract pays, which is the kind of thing a client says when the real reason is worse.

The ground problem here is the charge cycle. The Karyatid jumped in {ARRIVAL_HOURS} hours ago, and her jump sail is now feeding the drive coils. From the moment you board to a drive ready to jump is about {SPINUP_HOURS} hours, and nothing can speed that up. A JumpShip mid-charge cannot turn, run, or fight — it is a fixed structure with people inside it. So she is at her most takeable and her most fragile at the same time. A boarding party that seizes the bridge still has to hold it through the whole spin-up. Worse, the band's own DropShip, the Cinderfall, is clamped to the docking collar with most of the crew aboard her, not the JumpShip.

The deeper problem is the bond. Station rules forbid firing a weapon anywhere on the ring, and the operators treat a hull breach or a weapon signature the way a harbourmaster treats a fire. {NPC:intel-source} reports the Ash Company has paid its docking fees in full. By the bond's own logic, that makes the band the lawful guest and your unit the pirate the moment the shooting starts. Treat that as solid: the traffic log was copied at the purser's window six days ago.

objectives.primary: Take the Karyatid intact and fly her out of the anchorage under her own power to {EMPLOYER}'s meeting point, before the Ash Company can retake her or the operators can seize the dock.
objectives.secondary: Keep the station bond intact. Fire no weapon anyone can trace to you, kill no operators, and cause no breach that vents a pressurized section you need.
objectives.bonus: Take the Karyatid's navigation log intact. It holds eighteen months of the Ash Company's jump points, caches, and pirate-point routes — worth more than the hull to anyone who hunts raiders for a living.

complications.name: The Spin-Up Clock
complications.text: From the first boarder through the airlock to a drive ready to jump is about {SPINUP_HOURS} hours, and no order can shorten it. The whole mission is that gap: you have the ship, but it cannot leave yet.
complications.mechanicalEffect: A fixed countdown runs from boarding to jump-ready. The boarding team must hold the JumpShip's bridge and engineering against retake attempts for the full time. Cutting the charge to leave early scrubs the jump completely and strands the prize in the system.

complications.name: The Bond
complications.text: Fire a weapon on the ring and the operators log it as a breach of the bond. The blacklist that follows a flagged ship kills slower than any autocannon, and it reaches every port your unit still needs.
complications.mechanicalEffect: Any weapon discharge or hull breach traced to you inside the anchorage starts blacklist proceedings on the campaign layer. Boarding done with silent weapons, melee, or breaching tools rolls to see if it is traced back to you; anything louder is logged for certain.

complications.name: The Cinderfall at the Collar
complications.text: The Ash Company's DropShip is clamped to the Karyatid's docking collar, with most of the band aboard her, not the JumpShip. So the prize is lightly crewed, but a rested retake force is one airlock away.
complications.mechanicalEffect: Most of the band's strength is on the DropShip, not the target. Cutting or jamming the docking collar isolates the retake force, but it is a structural act the operators may notice. While the collar holds, fresh fighters can reach the JumpShip every cycle.

decisionPoints.name: How to Get Aboard
decisionPoints.context: The Karyatid is a lawful guest at a neutral dock, with a full crew rotation and a DropShip at her collar. There are three ways through her airlock, and each one costs you something different.

options.title: Walk On as Crew
advantages: Forged transfer papers and station coveralls put a boarding team aboard during the shift change, with no breach and no alarm
The bond stays clean because nothing happens the operators can log
The most time on the spin-up clock, because the team is inside before anyone contests the countdown
disadvantages: A handful of your people in coveralls against a JumpShip crew that knows its own faces
If one challenge goes wrong, the fight breaks out in the worst place: inside, outnumbered, with the Cinderfall one airlock away
No heavy weapon fits under a station coverall
options.consequence: The team gets aboard quietly, or it dies quietly. If the bluff holds all the way to the bridge, you own the ship before the band knows it has guests. If a face is recognized, it becomes a close-quarters knife fight against the clock, with no way to call in the rest of the unit without breaking the bond.

costs.resource: the bluff: forged station papers and a shift-change window that closes whether or not the team is ready
costs.risk: caught inside and outnumbered, with the bond forbidding the loud weapons that would even the odds

options.title: Hard Dock and Cut
advantages: Your own small craft mates to a side airlock and a breaching team cuts through with silent tools — controlled, rehearsed, and bringing real gear aboard
Sidesteps the crew-recognition problem entirely
A breaching charge on an inner hatch is far quieter than a weapon and may stay under the bond's limit
disadvantages: A hard dock at an unscheduled airlock is exactly the odd event the operators watch for
Cutting takes minutes the band may use to wake the Cinderfall
Any cut that vents a section is a logged breach, and the bond is gone
options.consequence: The team arrives with the tools to win the inside fight, but the approach shows up on the operators' board. The bond survives only if every cut stays sealed and quiet — and the noise of the breach gives the band its warning.

costs.resource: breaching stores and one small craft tied to the collar for the whole operation
costs.risk: an unscheduled hard dock flags the operators' board, and a vented section flags the bond

options.title: Buy the Berth Next to Her
advantages: Dock a chartered hauler in the next berth days ahead, legally, and let the boarding team cross at leisure through a maintenance gangway
The most patient option keeps both the bond and the surprise
Time to map the Karyatid's watch schedule before you commit a single person
disadvantages: A chartered berth and a crossing rig cost real money and {SETUP_DAYS} days the spin-up clock does not care about
Every day docked is a day the Ash Company might finish charging and simply leave on schedule
The berth charter is a paper trail back to your unit if anyone audits the dock later
options.consequence: You set things up in your favor and wait for the band's own charge cycle to open the window. The risk is the calendar: if the Karyatid charges faster than you can set up, the prize jumps out under its rightful thieves while you watch from the next berth.

costs.resource: {SETUP_DAYS} days of setting up early, plus a chartered hull whose manifest records that your unit was here
costs.risk: the Karyatid finishes her charge and leaves on schedule before your window opens

decisionPoints.name: The Collar Problem
decisionPoints.context: The bridge is taken and the spin-up clock is running. The Cinderfall is still clamped to the collar with the retake force aboard, and every cycle they push at the connecting airlock. You decide how to keep them off the JumpShip until she can jump.

options.title: Hold the Lock
advantages: Defend the connecting passage by position and barricade — no structural act, no risk to the bond
Keeps the Cinderfall's crew alive as prisoners or hostages, not corpses in a vented bay
The cleanest exit: the ship jumps with the collar intact and the band simply left behind
disadvantages: One defended passage against the bulk of the band, over and over, for the whole spin-up
Losses in the boarding team you cannot replace mid-operation
One thrown grenade or stray burst in the passage and the bond is forfeit anyway
options.consequence: The fight becomes a corridor held by exhausted boarders against a fresh crew that keeps coming. Win it and the Karyatid jumps with her former owners standing on the dock. Lose a few feet of corridor at the wrong moment and the retake force reaches engineering before the drive is ready.

costs.resource: the boarding team's whole strength held on one passage for the full {SPINUP_HOURS}-hour window
costs.risk: one loud weapon in the corridor voids the bond, and one lost barricade voids the prize

options.title: Sever the Collar
advantages: Blow the docking clamps and the Cinderfall drifts free with the retake force aboard, out of the fight in one stroke
The JumpShip is cut off for the rest of the spin-up, with no reinforcements possible
Fast and decisive, where holding the lock is slow and bloody
disadvantages: Cutting the clamps is plainly a structural act the operators will log, so the bond is almost certainly gone
A botched cut vents the collar passage and kills whoever is in it on both sides
A DropShip shoved off a charging JumpShip on the wrong heading may collide with other ships on the ring
options.consequence: The retake force is gone in a heartbeat, and so, probably, is the bond. You trade your standing at the only neutral port in the region for a clean spin-up — buying the prize and a blacklist in the same move.

costs.resource: the station bond, spent to buy an uninterrupted charge, with blacklist proceedings near-certain
costs.risk: a vented collar passage, or a bad push that endangers other docked ships, turns a blacklist into a manhunt

options.title: Take the Cinderfall Too
advantages: A second boarding team hits the DropShip while the band is fixed on retaking the JumpShip — take both ships and the band has nothing left to leave on
Doubles the prize and strands the whole Ash Company at the anchorage on foot
The richest possible outcome, if you have the strength to split
disadvantages: Splitting an already small boarding force across two ships invites losing both
Two inside fights at once double every chance of the loud shot that ends the bond
If the second team fails, it has only warned the DropShip crew and drained the force holding the JumpShip
options.consequence: The boldest play of the night: walk away with the band's entire spacelift and strand them on a neutral dock with no charter and no friends. It works only if both fights are won quietly and fast, and the spin-up clock waits for neither.

costs.resource: the boarding force split in two, with no reserve for either ship
costs.risk: two inside fights at once, two chances to break the bond, and a split force that can lose both prizes instead of taking one

entries.event: First boarder through the airlock. The spin-up clock starts. The Karyatid's drive coils are about {SPINUP_HOURS} hours from jump-ready and counting.
The bridge is contested. The watch crew raises the Cinderfall on the intercom before the team can cut the line, and the retake force starts to stir at the collar.
First retake push at the connecting airlock. Station operators send an 'unscheduled activity' query to the Karyatid's berth and wait for a reply your team must now fake.
The charge passes the point of no return. The drive cannot be safely shut down and restarted, so both sides are now locked into the jump window whatever happens at the dock.
Drive ready. The Karyatid can jump if you hold the bridge and engineering. Lose either one and she sits charged and trapped.

reactionTimeline.hardDeadline: The jump is your only way out. Hold the bridge and engineering when the drive comes ready at T+{SPINUP_HOURS}:00, and the Karyatid jumps — you win the instant she vanishes. If the retake force holds either the bridge or engineering at that moment, the prize is a charged JumpShip you cannot fly, at a dock you can no longer claim, with the operators already drafting the blacklist.

opforSketch.composition: The Ash Company afloat: a raider crew of {BAND_CREW} aboard the Cinderfall (Regular boarders, Veteran in their own corridors), plus a light JumpShip watch on the Karyatid (Green). Shipboard weapons only — needlers, blades, breaching tools, vacuum suits; the bond forbids anything heavier and the band knows the bond better than the unit does. No 'Mechs aboard the charging ship, but the Cinderfall's bay holds 2-3 light salvage 'Mechs the band can deploy onto the ring if the operation spills outside the bond and the gloves come off. Generator should keep the interior fight infantry-scale and reserve any 'Mech action for the campaign layer once the bond breaks.
opforSketch.behavior: The band fights to retake its mobile home, not to die for it: aggressive probes at the collar lock, conservative when bled, and quick to flip from defense to flight the moment the JumpShip is clearly lost. They will not break the bond first — it is their livelihood too — but once the unit breaks it, they answer with everything in the Cinderfall's bay and a grudge that travels by courier.

forks.name: OPERATION CLEAN PAPER
forks.trigger: The Karyatid jumps out intact with the navigation log aboard and the bond unbroken.
forks.consequence: The log maps the Ash Company's whole pattern: caches, pirate points, and the buyer who fences their salvage. {EMPLOYER} funds a follow-on strike on one named cache before the band can reroute, and the unit jumps to a coordinate no honest chart shows.

forks.name: OPERATION BLACKLISTED
forks.trigger: The bond breaks, or the prize is lost and the unit is logged as the attacker.
forks.consequence: The anchorage operators flag the unit to every port on the circuit, and the Ash Company — now homeless or just furious — knows exactly who came for its ship. The unit has to run the band down in open space to clear its name, and the region's only recharge station will no longer service its ships.

forks.name: OPERATION DEAD WEIGHT
forks.trigger: The unit holds the Karyatid but the spin-up is scrubbed, leaving her charged but trapped in the system.
forks.consequence: The prize is a JumpShip that cannot leave, clamped at a dock the operators are moving to seize, with the band regrouping and a buyer on the way. The unit now defends a fortune it cannot fly while three parties close on the one berth it cannot leave.

storyElementSeed: On the Karyatid's bridge, taken and quiet, a boarder watches the drive-charge gauge crawl toward green. The needle does not move any faster for courage. Four hours of charge left, and a door behind him that keeps trying to open.

resourceGates.appliesTo: Buy the Berth Next to Her
resourceGates.lackingText: No reserve for a pre-positioning charter: the adjacent berth must be sub-leased through a broker at a premium — add 14,000 C-bills and a middleman who now knows the unit wanted a berth next to a pirate's ship.

No owned small craft to mate the collar: the hard dock runs on a hired station tender whose pilot is on the operators' payroll — add 8,000 C-bills and accept that the approach is witnessed by exactly the wrong person.

title: OPERATION LONG TALLY
skeleton: a reconnaissance element must locate a raider band whose base is unknown but whose supply tramp is followable, tracing the resupply ship port by port through a frontier circuit to backtrack the hidden lair, where the band itself is never the quarry until the trail ends and arriving after the tramp has turned around loses the thread for a season
inspiration: Battle of the Atlantic convoy-route reconstruction; tracing a blockade-runner's supply chain back to its base
situation:
Nobody has found the Greel band's base in three years of trying, and {EMPLOYER} has stopped paying people to search for it head-on. The band raids a six-system frontier arc and then vanishes — no transit logs, no pirate-point fix, no captured crew who knows more than his own deck. But everyone on the arc knows the Patient Maud: a battered Buccaneer-class DropShip with a forged Lyran registry. She calls at the arc's frontier ports on a slow, irregular loop, buying the things a raider band cannot make for itself — reactor coolant, autocannon stock, medical supplies, bulk rations. {NPC:intel-source} is sure the Maud is the Greel band's supply ship. She is not sure of much else, and her port-call reports come from four harbourmasters and run twelve to forty days old.

{EMPLOYER}, through {NPC:employer-contact}, has hired your unit for the one thing a long, patient tail can do that a dozen frantic searches could not: follow the Maud's supply run backward to the base it feeds. The band is not the target. The ship is. Every port she visits, every cargo she loads, every course she sets is one more mark on the map, and enough marks draw a line that ends at the base.

The ground problem is the circuit itself: a string of {ARC_PORTS} lightly governed frontier ports across the arc. Each is its own territory, and each has a harbourmaster who sells information to whoever asks and warns whoever pays more. There has been no central traffic authority since the Blackout. The only way to learn where the Maud went is to be at the next port when she arrives, or to buy the answer from someone who will also sell your interest in her to the next buyer. Reading the chain means moving along it faster than she does without ever being seen to follow.

The clock is the loop. {NPC:intel-source} figures the Maud is about {LOOP_REMAINING} weeks from finishing her buying and turning back toward the base. Once she runs for home, a tail that has not already traced her back is left holding a list of ports and no destination — waiting a full loop, maybe a season, for the pattern to repeat. You are rebuilding a route that is being walked away from you in real time.

objectives.primary: Find the Greel band's base by tracing the Patient Maud's supply run to its source. Deliver a confirmed system and a usable line of approach — intelligence an assault force can act on.
objectives.secondary: Read the chain without tipping it off. The Maud must reach home not knowing she was followed, so the base is still there and still unready when your intelligence is used.
objectives.bonus: Identify the band's fence and support network along the arc — the ports, harbourmasters, and brokers that keep the Maud supplied — so the base is not just found but cut off.

complications.name: The Selling Ports
complications.text: Every harbourmaster on the arc sells information, including who is asking after the Patient Maud. The same window that tells you where she went tells her who wants to know.
complications.mechanicalEffect: Each port inquiry moves the trail forward and rolls against a band-awareness track. Buying data raises that track faster than quiet watching does. Push the track too high and the Maud changes her loop or runs for home early, and you lose the trail.

complications.name: The Turning Loop
complications.text: The Maud is about {LOOP_REMAINING} weeks from finishing her buying and heading home. A tail that has not traced her back by then loses the thread until the pattern repeats, a full loop away.
complications.mechanicalEffect: A loop clock runs in weeks. If the base is not found before the Maud turns for home, the trail resets. The contract must then either wait a full loop or go ahead on a partial, low-confidence fix.

complications.name: Cold Cargo, Hot Cargo
complications.text: The Maud buys dull things in dull amounts, and a cargo list is not proof. Some of her loads really are for honest charter work her forged registry actually runs. That cover makes the real pattern hard to read from any one port.
complications.mechanicalEffect: Not every port call is a supply run for the band; some are ordinary cover traffic. Read a cover call as a band call and the trail heads down a false branch, costing days and confidence. Telling them apart means cross-checking manifests from several ports, not trusting a single one.

decisionPoints.name: How to Follow
decisionPoints.context: The Maud is somewhere ahead on her loop of frontier ports, buying her way home. You decide how to read the chain — and how much money, and how much risk of being seen, you will spend to read it fast enough.

options.title: Shadow Her Ship
advantages: Keep your own ship one jump behind the Maud and watch her port calls yourself — no harbourmaster paid, no inquiry logged
The cleanest read: what she really loads and where she really goes, seen with your own eyes
The smallest band-awareness footprint, as long as your tail discipline holds
disadvantages: One jump behind means arriving after she has left, reading her wake, not her deck — and risking the jump she does not signal ahead
A warship-sized ship appearing one jump behind a trader, port after port, is a pattern a careful supply officer will eventually notice
Recharge cycles mean you cannot always keep pace, and one missed jump loses her
options.consequence: You read the chain firsthand and pay for it in the gaps a recharge clock opens. Hold the tail and the trail is clean and damning. Lose one jump to a charge cycle and the Maud is a port ahead and gone, and you can only pick up the thread by going back to buying answers.

costs.resource: your own travel schedule, bent to a trader's irregular route with no room for a missed jump
costs.risk: the same ship one jump behind at six ports is a tail any careful supply officer eventually reads

options.title: Buy the Harbourmasters
advantages: Pay ahead at the ports the Maud is likely to call, so her movements get reported the moment she arrives — coverage your unit cannot give every port on its own
Fast: the trail moves at the speed of paid eyes, not one shadowing ship
Frees you to jump straight to the base once the pattern is clear, instead of trailing the whole loop
disadvantages: Every harbourmaster you pay is a harbourmaster who can be paid more to warn the Maud
Frontier port data is a market, and your interest in one ship is itself for sale — someone will sell it
Paid reports are thin: arrivals and departures, not cargoes or courses
options.consequence: You buy a wide, fast, shallow picture and accept that the band may learn it is being watched. The trail comes together quickly from a dozen ports at once — but the Maud may turn for home early, or worse, lead your paid-for tail to a base the band has had time to prepare for visitors.

costs.resource: the band-awareness track: a paid network the band can outbid one harbourmaster at a time
costs.risk: your target, and your interest in it, are both for sale at every port you pay

options.title: Plant a Beacon
advantages: Get a hidden tracker aboard the Maud at one port — a bribed dock worker, a tagged crate, a beacon clamped to the hull — and her own jumps report her course home
The decisive read: not where she has been, but where she is going, straight to the base
Once planted, the trail needs no more inquiries and no shadowing ship
disadvantages: Getting a device aboard means a person aboard or alongside her, at one port, in one window, with one chance
A supply ship for a nervous band may sweep for exactly this before every jump home
A found beacon does more than fail. It tells the band, plainly, that someone is hunting the base, and turns an unready lair into a waiting one
options.consequence: The highest-value and highest-risk read on the board. A clean plant hands you the base coordinate the moment the Maud jumps for it. A blown plant hands the band the one thing it has protected for three years — the knowledge that it has been found — and the assault that follows lands on ground the band has prepared.

costs.resource: one planting window at one port, with your whole intelligence picture riding on whether the device is found before the jump home
costs.risk: getting caught does not just lose the trail — it arms the destination, turning an unready base into an ambush

decisionPoints.name: The Branch Point
decisionPoints.context: The chain splits. At the third port the Maud's trail forks: a cargo went one way under her name, her ship went another. One branch is the band's resupply; the other is ordinary cover charter. You are not sure which is which, and the loop clock does not pause while you decide.

options.title: Follow the Cargo
advantages: The supplies are what feed the band, so tracing the coolant and autocannon stock follows the need, not the disguise
Cargo manifests can be cross-checked across ports — a case you can build and test
If the cargo leads home, you get the base and the supply route both
disadvantages: The cargo may be handed off through a middleman on purpose, to break the trail at the band's end
Following freight means leaving the Maud's ship unwatched — if she was the real thread, she is gone
Extra handoffs add middlemen who eat up the loop clock
options.consequence: You bet the band is found by what it uses. If the cargo runs to the base, the case is complete and backed by two sources. If it dead-ends at a fence's warehouse while the Maud quietly carried the real load herself, you have spent your best weeks on a decoy and the ship is over the horizon.

costs.resource: 8 days of the loop clock spent tracing freight that may be a deliberate dead-end
costs.risk: a middleman handoff breaks the cargo trail right where it mattered, and the ship you stopped watching is gone

options.title: Follow the Ship
advantages: The ship is the constant — wherever the Maud goes, the band's supply run goes with her
Keeps you on the one target you can actually track and intercept
A ship cannot be handed off to a middleman; she is where she is
disadvantages: If this leg was cover charter, you follow the Maud on honest business and learn nothing about the base
The real resupply cargo, left unwatched, reaches the band with no mark against it
A wasted leg may be the leg that runs the loop clock out
options.consequence: You stay with the ship and trust that the ship is the answer. Guess right and the Maud walks you to the base's doorstep. Guess wrong and you spend the decisive weeks escorting a trader through legitimate ports while the band restocks unseen and the loop runs down.

costs.resource: 6 days of the loop clock spent on a ship that may be running cover this leg
costs.risk: following honest charter traffic while the real resupply reaches the band untracked

options.title: Split and Read Both
advantages: Send a detachment after the cargo and keep the main body on the ship — read both branches and settle the fork for certain
Removes the guess: whichever branch leads home, you are on it
Reading both branches also exposes the middleman network for the bonus objective
disadvantages: Splitting a recon force across two territories halves your strength if either branch turns hostile
Two parties asking questions at two ports double the band-awareness footprint
Meeting back up across frontier jumps with no working HPG is its own gamble — a detachment can be stranded a loop away
options.consequence: The thorough answer at twice the exposure. You read the whole fork and learn which branch is real and how the band hides the other. The price is a split force, a louder footprint, and the standing risk that a detachment chases a decoy and cannot rejoin before the base is hit.

costs.resource: the recon force split across two territories, with no working HPG to coordinate the reunion
costs.risk: twice the awareness footprint, and a detachment that can be stranded a full loop from the main effort

entries.event: The trail opens: the Patient Maud is confirmed at the arc's third port, loading cargo. The loop clock is about {LOOP_REMAINING} weeks from her turn for home.
The Maud's manifest is logged at the harbourmaster's window — and within a day, a second party is noticed asking after the same ship. Your unit is not the only one reading these windows.
Band-awareness check. If your footprint has grown too loud, the Maud breaks her pattern — an unscheduled jump, a skipped port — and you must pick up the trail cold.
The Maud finishes her buying. This is her last port call before the run home, and the final chance to read her outbound course unless a planted beacon is already your only fix.
The Maud jumps for home. Either you have the base coordinate, or you have a list of ports and a season's wait for the loop to come around again.

reactionTimeline.hardDeadline: The deadline is the Maud's turn for home, about {LOOP_REMAINING} weeks out. Find the base before she runs and you hand {EMPLOYER} a coordinate and a clean approach. Miss it and the trail goes cold with the ship, leaving you a list of frontier ports, a band that may now know it was hunted, and a full loop — a season or more — before the pattern shows the thread again.

opforSketch.composition: The Greel band's logistics afloat: the Patient Maud, a Buccaneer-class DropShip (forged registry, civilian crew of {MAUD_CREW}, Green as fighters, Veteran as smugglers), unarmed by design — her defense is invisibility, not guns. The band proper is offscreen until the base is found: estimated 1 reinforced raider company of mixed salvage 'Mechs and technicals (Regular) plus the base's fixed defenses, fielded only if the trail is blown and the band turns to defend or to hunt the hunters. Generator should keep this mission's on-table contact light and intelligence-driven; the real fight is the assault this recon enables, on the campaign layer.
opforSketch.behavior: The Maud runs like a smuggler, not a warship: never the same loop twice exactly, never a straight line home, and gone at the first sign of a tail. Her crew fights only if cornered and then only to buy a jump. The band behind her is patient and invisible by policy — its single greatest asset is that nobody knows where it lives, and it will spend cargo, ports, and even the Maud herself to keep it that way the moment it learns it has been read.

forks.name: OPERATION SHORT TALLY
forks.trigger: The base is found with a clean approach and the trail still unblown.
forks.consequence: {EMPLOYER} turns the intelligence into the raid it was always meant for. The unit jumps on the Greel base while it sits unready, the supply route mapped and the defenses known, with the Patient Maud still inbound carrying supplies the band will never get to use.

forks.name: OPERATION COLD TRAIL
forks.trigger: The Maud turns for home unfollowed, or the trail breaks on a decoy branch.
forks.consequence: The thread is lost with the ship. {EMPLOYER} will not pay for a full loop's wait. The next job is a colder, harder search that starts from the band's next raid — from the wreckage of a strike instead of the supply run that fed it.

forks.name: OPERATION SPRUNG TRAP
forks.trigger: The band learns it has been traced — a found beacon, a harbourmaster's warning, a tail seen once too often.
forks.consequence: The base coordinate, when it comes, points to ground the band has had time to prepare or abandon. The unit either assaults an ambush dressed as a base, or chases a band that has lifted everything and scattered. Either way, the Greel supply crew now hunts the hunters along the same arc.

storyElementSeed: A frontier harbourmaster's window, late. The clerk slides a copied manifest across the counter and takes the money. Then, smiling, he mentions for free that a polite man asked after the very same ship three days ago — and would you like to know what that man paid.

LOOP_REMAINING.unit: weeks until the tramp turns home

resourceGates.lackingText: No owned JumpShip to keep pace: the shadow runs on hired transit booked one jump at a time, and a hired captain will not chase a tramp into an uncharted jump — add 15,000 C-bills and accept the gaps the schedule forces.

Insufficient operating cash to pre-pay the network: coverage shrinks to 3 of the arc's ports, leaving gaps in the loop the Maud can slip through unobserved — and the unpaid harbourmasters notice who could not afford them.

title: OPERATION FALSE SPRING
skeleton: an extraction element must lift a defecting raider navigator who alone holds the route to a hidden base out of a pirate harbour-town during a festival truce, where the crowd is the only cover and the defector will not move until his dependents are clear too, so the snatch is paced by getting the family out first under a peace that ends at a fixed hour
inspiration: a defector exfiltration timed to a holiday amnesty; the navigator who sells the only chart
situation:
Once a year the harbour-town the raiders call Sprat's Landing declares the Slack: a festival truce that has held for a generation, because even pirates need one week where nobody settles scores. Crews come ashore, weapons are locked away, feuds are put on hold, and the whole anchorage gets drunk and dances on the tide flats while the fleet rides at anchor. It is the only week the town is not a fortress, and the only week your contact can move.

The contact is a navigator the raiders call Pell. He has plotted jumps for the Korrigan band for six years and wants out before the band's luck runs out. What makes him worth a contract is the route in his head: the Korrigan base sits at a pirate point no survey shows, reachable only by a jump solution Pell carries. The band guards him with his life, because his life is their guarantee. {EMPLOYER}, through {NPC:employer-contact}, wants Pell and the route. {NPC:intel-source} confirms the offer is real and the danger is too. Pell's last message was hand-carried out nine days ago, at the cost of the courier's thumb.

The ground problem is the tide flats. Sprat's Landing sits on a shallow coastal shelf. At low tide it drains into kilometers of mud that the festival spills across — bonfires, market stalls, beached boats. At high tide it floods back into a working harbour. The festival lives on the flats at low water. The only ground a DropShip can land on, the old salt-barge hard, is reachable across the flats and only between tides. So your window is not just the Slack — it is the hours of low water inside the Slack, when the crowd is thickest and the ground is dry.

Here is what makes it a snatch and not a handshake: Pell will not leave alone. His sister and her two children live in the town under the band's eye, on purpose, so that Pell stays bought. He will not jump for {EMPLOYER} knowing the band will make them pay for it. So it is four people, not one: a navigator who is watched, and three dependents held as the band's insurance. All four must move through a festival crowd to a tidal landing ground, under a truce that ends — by tradition, at an exact hour the band counts to — at the turn of the week.

objectives.primary: Get the navigator Pell and the jump solution to the Korrigan base off Sprat's Landing and clear of the band, alive and willing, before the Slack ends.
objectives.secondary: Bring out Pell's three dependents — his sister and her two children — unharmed. A navigator who arrives having watched his family die is a navigator who gives you nothing useful.
objectives.bonus: Leave the Slack truce intact and the band unsure who took Pell. A clean disappearance the Korrigans cannot pin on {EMPLOYER} keeps the festival open as a way back in later.

complications.name: The Watched Man
complications.text: Pell is the band's route home, and the band knows it. Even during the Slack he has a minder or two — relaxed and drunk, but there — because a navigator is the one asset a raider band never lets fully off the leash.
complications.mechanicalEffect: Pell cannot just walk to the pickup; his minders must be pulled away, distracted, or taken out quietly. Any open move on Pell himself turns the festival crowd from cover into a mob and ends the truce early.

complications.name: The Insurance Family
complications.text: The sister and her children are housed away from Pell, on purpose, so no single move frees all four. Move the family first and you warn the band its leverage is walking. Move Pell first and you leave hostages for the reprisal he defected to prevent.
complications.mechanicalEffect: The dependents and the navigator are in separate places and must be extracted in order. Whichever you move first raises the alarm risk for the second. Leaving any dependent behind lowers Pell's cooperation and the intelligence you get on the campaign layer.

complications.name: The Turning Tide
complications.text: The salt-barge hard is dry ground only between tides, and the festival crowd that hides your team thins as the water comes back. Your window is where low water and the Slack overlap, and both are running out.
complications.mechanicalEffect: The usable window is the overlap of two things: the low-tide hard being dry, and the festival crowd being present. As the tide turns, the landing ground floods and the cover clears at the same time. Miss the window and you wait a full tide cycle the truce clock may not allow.

decisionPoints.name: The Order of the Lift
decisionPoints.context: Four people, two locations, one tide. The band has set things up so no single clean move frees them all. You decide the order, knowing each choice raises the alarm risk for whatever comes second.

options.title: Family First, Quietly
advantages: Move the sister and children out under festival cover while the band watches Pell, not them — the dependents are the half no one guards closely
Once the family is clear, Pell jumps without hesitation and the reprisal threat is gone
The kindest order, and the one Pell himself will trust
disadvantages: A navigator whose family quietly vanishes may stop looking afraid, and his minders will notice — his face could give the game away before the team reaches him
Three people including children move through a crowd slower and more visibly than one
If the family lift snags, Pell is still watched and now the band is alert
options.consequence: You free the leverage before reaching for the prize. Done cleanly, Pell walks to the landing ground a free man and the band realizes too late. Done slowly, the gap between the family vanishing and Pell moving is exactly the window a sober minder uses to raise the alarm.

costs.resource: the timing gap between the family getting clear and Pell moving — every minute of it, his minders might read his face
costs.risk: a navigator who has stopped being afraid is a tell, and the band watches him for exactly that

options.title: Simultaneous Snatch
advantages: Two teams move on Pell and the family at the same moment — no warning gap, no order for the band to read
Both halves come out clear together, or get caught together, so no hostages are left for a reprisal
The fastest use of the low-tide window
disadvantages: Splitting the force across two locations in a hostile town halves your strength at each
Two moves at once double the chance one trips the alarm — and an alarm at either place ends the truce for both
Coordinating across a festival crowd on locked-down comms is its own hazard
options.consequence: The whole operation in one held breath: both teams move, both prizes come out together, and the band has no sequence to interrupt. It works if both snatches stay quiet to the same second. If either is seen, you have started two fights in a pirate town at once, with the tide already turning.

costs.resource: the force split two ways, with no reserve for either location
costs.risk: two snatches at once, two chances to end the truce, and a split force that can lose both

options.title: Pell First, Hold the Family
advantages: Take the navigator the moment the window opens — the prize is secured before anything can go wrong with the harder, slower family lift
A second team covers the dependents in place, ready to move them out or shield them the instant Pell is clear
Guarantees the intelligence even if the family lift turns into a fight
disadvantages: Taking Pell first leaves his family, for a while, as exactly the hostages the band will reach for — and Pell knows it and may refuse to move without them
If the family lift then fails, you have the route and a navigator who will never forgive you or fully cooperate
The covering team on the family is locked into a reprisal fight on the band's terms if the alarm goes
options.consequence: The cold-blooded order: secure the asset, then save the people. It guarantees {EMPLOYER} the route but gambles the family on a second lift under an alarm Pell's own absence may have raised — the bonus and the secondary both riding on a fight you chose to risk.

costs.resource: the family's safety, held second behind the route for the length of one lift
costs.risk: Pell taken first leaves his family the reprisal target for the gap before they too are clear

decisionPoints.name: The Tide and the Truce
decisionPoints.context: The order of the lift is set, but the landing ground is the salt-barge hard, dry only at low water, and the Slack ends at a fixed hour the band counts to. Getting four people across the flats to the DropShip is its own problem, and the two clocks do not line up cleanly.

options.title: Cross at Low Water, Lift Before the Tide
advantages: Move everyone across the dry flats while the festival crowd is thickest and the ground is hard — the most cover and a solid landing ground
The DropShip lands and lifts on dry ground with the band still drunk and the truce still holding
The by-the-book window, used exactly as intended
disadvantages: The low-water window is short, and the crowd that hides the team also clogs the route to the hard
A DropShip on the salt-barge hard during the festival is visible to the whole town the moment it lands, so the disappearance is no longer clean
Cut it too fine on the tide and the hard floods under a loaded ship
options.consequence: The team rides the festival's own rhythm out: across the flats with the crowd, onto a dry hard, and up before the water returns. The truce holds if the ship is gone before anyone sober asks why a DropShip landed at a festival — and the tide gives no grace for a late lift.

costs.resource: the low-water window: a short stretch of dry ground the loaded lift must clear before the sea returns
costs.risk: a DropShip on the hard in daylight at the festival makes the snatch visible even if no shot is fired

options.title: Boat Out to a Ship Offshore
advantages: Move the four by small boat off the flats to a DropShip waiting offshore or in a quiet cove — no landing in the town at all
Keeps the lift out of sight: the band sees a festival, not a landing
Skips the tide-locked hard entirely
disadvantages: Four people including children in a small boat off a fast-current coast is dangerous, and slower than a ground lift
A boat leaving during the Slack is less alarming than a DropShip, but not nothing — fishing-boat movements get watched out of habit
The transfer at sea, boat to DropShip, is a fragile minute with no cover at all
options.consequence: The quiet professional's exit: off the flats by water, onto a ship that never touched the town. The disappearance is clean and deniable if the boat is not marked. But the sea adds its own risk to a cargo of one navigator and two children, and a swamped boat loses everything the contract is for.

costs.resource: a small-boat run off a fast-current coast with children aboard, and an exposed boat-to-ship transfer at the end
costs.risk: the sea is a hazard the festival is not, and a botched boat-to-ship transfer loses the prize with no enemy needed

options.title: Stage a Festival Incident
advantages: Set a controlled distraction — a stall fire, a staged brawl, a beached boat breaking loose — to pull the crowd and the minders away from both the route and the hard
Opens clear lanes through the crush at the exact moment of the lift
Turns the festival's chaos from a problem into a tool
disadvantages: Any incident during the Slack risks being read as breaking the truce — and a broken truce brings the whole town's locked-away weapons back out at once
A distraction that gets out of hand becomes a riot the team has to escape through
If the staging is traced to your unit, the clean disappearance is gone and the band has a grudge with an address
options.consequence: The team makes its own window in the festival's chaos. A clean incident opens the lanes and the four are gone before order returns. An incident that tips into a broken truce ends the Slack early, arms the anchorage, and turns your exit into a fighting withdrawal across flooding flats.

costs.resource: the truce's stability, gambled on a distraction staying just a distraction
costs.risk: an incident read as breaking the truce brings every locked-away weapon in the town back into play at once

entries.event: Low water inside the Slack. The festival is at its peak on the flats, the salt-barge hard is dry, and the window is open. Pell is in the crowd with two minders; the family is housed three streets up.
First team reaches the family. Whatever order you chose, the alarm clock for the band's leverage starts the moment the dependents move.
The tide turns. The outer flats start to wet and the crowd drifts up off the lowest ground. The usable landing ground and the cover both shrink from the seaward edge.
The Slack's traditional end nears. The band's criers start calling crews back to order, and locked-away weapons come off the racks by custom, truce or no truce.
High water and the truce's end arrive together. The hard is under the sea, the festival is over, and the anchorage is a fortress again with every gun back in hand.

reactionTimeline.hardDeadline: Your window is where low water and the Slack overlap, and both close by T+4:00 — the sea takes the hard and tradition ends the truce in the same hour. Get all four clear of Sprat's Landing before that mark and you deliver a navigator, a route, and a family with the band none the wiser. Anyone still ashore when the water and the criers come in is stuck in a pirate town with the festival over, the weapons drawn, and the one man who could have bought their way out now the reason the whole anchorage is hunting.

opforSketch.composition: The Korrigan band ashore for the Slack: most of a raider company at rest — {BAND_ASHORE} crew, weapons bonded by truce, drunk and scattered through the festival (Green while bonded and partying, Regular the instant the truce breaks and the racks open). Pell's minders: 2-3 sober-ish hands keeping a navigator in sight. The band's real teeth — salvage 'Mechs and technicals — sit at the bonded anchorage and the town's hardstand, fielded only if the truce breaks and the band mobilizes. Generator should keep the festival phase infantry-scale and reserve 'Mech contact for a blown-truce withdrawal on the campaign layer.
opforSketch.behavior: Under the Slack the band is a crowd, not a force — relaxed, off-guard, and genuinely invested in the truce that lets them rest. They will not mobilize over a quiet disappearance until someone connects it to Pell. But a broken truce or an overt snatch flips the whole anchorage at once: the racks open, the 'Mechs warm, and a band that lives by never letting its navigator go turns the entire town into a cordon around the flats.

forks.name: OPERATION TRUE NORTH
forks.trigger: Pell and the route are extracted, the family is clear, and the truce is left intact.
forks.consequence: Pell's jump solution opens the Korrigan base to {EMPLOYER}, and a grateful navigator plots the approach himself. The unit jumps on a pirate point no chart shows, against a band that does not yet know its only door has a key cut for it.

forks.name: OPERATION SALT WAKE
forks.trigger: The truce breaks, the window is missed, or Pell is lost or taken back.
forks.consequence: The Korrigans know a navigator was the target and answer the only way a raider band can. Pell's value dies with his usefulness, the base route is changed, and any of the family left behind becomes the band's message. The next job is a hard rescue of whoever is still alive, with the festival door closed for good.

forks.name: OPERATION BROKEN SLACK
forks.trigger: The snatch succeeds but the truce is plainly broken and traced to the unit.
forks.consequence: Sprat's Landing's generation-old festival is dead, and the harbour-towns of the arc know who killed it. Your unit is now the outfit that broke the Slack, unwelcome at every pirate port that runs one. {EMPLOYER}'s prize is secured at the cost of your access to the whole frontier underworld you just learned to work.

storyElementSeed: On the tide flats at low water, a navigator dances badly in a borrowed coat, laughing too loud for a man with two minders. Three streets up, a woman packs nothing, because packing would give her away, and tells her children they are going to see the big ships. One of them believes her.

resourceGates.appliesTo: Boat Out to a Ship Offshore
resourceGates.lackingText: No owned DropShip to wait offshore: the standoff lift runs on a chartered coastal lighter rendezvousing with a hired ship beyond the headland — add 11,000 C-bills and a charter crew who will talk about the strange cargo they carried for the rest of the season.

No local staging cell: the distraction must be improvised with hired festival hands who do not know what they are setting up — add 5,000 C-bills and the standing risk that a paid stranger talks the moment the band asks who lit the fire.

title: OPERATION DEEP CHORUS
skeleton: a small force must fake a working comms-relay restoration on a dead world convincingly enough to draw every raider band in the region to converge on a prize that does not exist, so the real traffic moves through emptied lanes, where the deception must hold past the point the predators commit and the element must then escape the very greed it summoned before the bands realize the prize is a stage set
inspiration: Operation Fortitude / Quicksilver — the phantom army and the inflatable order of battle, 1944
situation:
In the comms blackout the Blackout left behind, a working HPG is the most valuable rumor in the Inner Sphere, and {EMPLOYER} means to spend that rumor like a coin. The real problem is this: {EMPLOYER} has to move something through the {DISTRICT} frontier lanes — a convoy, a cadre, a payment, the brief does not say and your unit was wise not to ask — past a region thick with raider bands who watch those lanes for exactly that kind of traffic. The answer is a lie on a planetary scale.

The stage is a dead world: a frontier system whose small colony failed years ago, where a Star League-era HPG compound still stands on the dust plain, intact-looking and completely silent. {EMPLOYER}, through {NPC:employer-contact}, has hired your unit to make that compound look like it is coming back to life — a secret repair project, heavily but clumsily guarded, leaking exactly the right rumors to exactly the right ears. The goal is not to defend anything. The goal is to make every greedy band in the region believe a working HPG is about to exist, race to the dead world to grab it, and in doing so pull their watch off the lanes {EMPLOYER}'s real traffic needs for {DECOY_DAYS} days.

The ground problem is the dust plain itself. The HPG compound sits in the open on a flat pan with one road in, ringed by low dunes {DUNE_RANGE} kilometers out. The openness is the point: the repair work must be seen, the guard force must be countable, and the activity must look real to a band scouting from the dune line. But the same openness that sells the lie traps the ones selling it. A force that has spent days faking strength on an exposed pan has nowhere to hide when the bands it summoned arrive for real, and the dunes that hid the scouts will hide the attack.

Here is what makes it deadly: {NPC:intel-source} confirms at least {BAND_COUNT} separate bands are likely to take the bait, and they do not work together. The scout-traffic estimates come from three frontier ports and run eight to twenty-five days old. A diversion that works too well does not draw one band you can handle — it draws several at once, racing each other for a prize that will turn out to be a stage set. You must be gone before the first of them gets close enough to see the fakes behind the curtain.

objectives.primary: Keep the deception going for {DECOY_DAYS} days — long enough that the region's raider bands commit to the dead world and pull their watch off the lanes {EMPLOYER}'s real traffic uses — then get the deception force out intact.
objectives.secondary: Draw and pin as many bands as possible on the dead world without getting into a decisive fight. Every band racing here is a band off the lanes, and a band that arrives is worth more pinned than fought.
objectives.bonus: Get clear before any band figures out the HPG is a fake. A trick the raiders never realize was a trick keeps the dead world usable as bait again and protects the lanes well past this one operation.

complications.name: Selling Strength You Lack
complications.text: The guard force has to look worth fighting through — large, organized, protecting something real — while staying small enough to pull out fast. Every prop that sells the lie is a prop that cannot fight.
complications.mechanicalEffect: The deception force looks far stronger than it really is — decoy emplacements, staged activity, dummy units in the narrative layer. Bands commit based on how strong it looks; you survive based on how strong it actually is. That gap is the whole risk.

complications.name: The Uncoordinated Swarm
complications.text: At least {BAND_COUNT} bands may bite, and they answer to no one. They will not arrive together or politely — they will race each other, and a prize several bands all want is one they will eventually fight each other over.
complications.mechanicalEffect: Several separate enemy groups arrive on staggered, uncontrolled timelines. They may fight each other as readily as they fight you, but you cannot count on it. Each band's arrival raises the pressure, and a late extraction risks being caught between two of them.

complications.name: The Curtain
complications.text: The HPG is a stage set, and a stage set only holds up from a distance. Any band that gets close enough, or any scout that gets inside, sees fake tanks and dead consoles. An exposed trick is worse than no trick, because a humiliated band hunts for spite.
complications.mechanicalEffect: Close scouting and infiltration attempts roll against how well the deception holds. Once it breaks, that band switches from racing for a prize to hunting the tricksters, and the region's bands learn the lanes were the real target — which lowers how well this trick works next time.

decisionPoints.name: How Big to Make the Lie
decisionPoints.context: The lie has to be loud enough to pull bands off the lanes, but quiet enough that you can still get out. You set the size of the deception, knowing a bigger lie draws more raiders and digs a deeper hole to climb out of.

options.title: A Modest Restoration
advantages: Stage a small, believable effort — a few techs, a light guard, careful rumor — that draws the nearer, hungrier bands without calling in the whole region
Easy to pull out of: a small setup comes down fast
Less exposure if a scout gets close, because there is less to disprove
disadvantages: A modest prize may not pull the larger, more disciplined bands off rich lanes — they may decide it is not worth the trip
Fewer bands drawn means more bands still watching the lanes the real traffic needs
Underselling risks the whole point: a diversion nobody diverts to is just a unit camping on a dust plain
options.consequence: You tell a small lie and accept that small lies move small crowds. The nearer bands take the bait and the lanes clear part of the way. The disciplined raiders stay put, and {EMPLOYER}'s traffic runs a gauntlet that is thinner but not empty.

costs.resource: the reach of the trick: a modest prize the larger bands may sensibly ignore
costs.risk: a diversion too small to pull the bands that matter leaves the real lanes still watched

options.title: A Major Project
advantages: Stage a large, convincing repair effort — a heavy staged guard, visible specialist arrivals, rumor seeded at every port — that no band can afford to let a rival grab
Pulls the most bands off the lanes, clearing them almost entirely
The disciplined raiders come too: a working HPG is worth dropping any raid for
disadvantages: A major project draws the major bands — the very forces most able to overrun your deception force if the extraction slips
More props, more staged strength, more to disprove, and more to bring down when you pull out
Several strong bands arriving at once on an exposed pan is the EXTREME-threat version of this operation
options.consequence: You tell the biggest lie you can and call the whole region's greed to one dead world. The lanes go quiet and {EMPLOYER}'s traffic sails clean — but your deception force sits on an open pan with several raider companies racing toward it and a stage set that will not survive a close look.

costs.resource: the size of the trap, which is also the size of the force now racing to spring it on you
costs.risk: the more the diversion succeeds, the more dangerous the extraction — several strong bands, one exposed pan

options.title: A Project With Real Teeth
advantages: Stage the repair effort but back it with real combat strength — make it a prize the bands must actually fight for, and bleed them when they try
Turns the diversion into attrition: bands that commit don't just leave the lanes, they lose strength on the pan
A real defense buys time and gives you a fighting way out that the pure-bluff versions lack
disadvantages: Real teeth mean a real garrison you cannot easily pull out — committing strength to the bluff undercuts the whole 'small footprint, fast exit' plan
Fighting hard for the compound risks giving away that it is a stage set when the bands break in and find nothing
Drawing bands into a real fight drags you into the decisive battle you were supposed to avoid
options.consequence: The middle path, with the highest body count. You make the lie defensible and punish the greedy, at the cost of a heavier force tied to an exposed position. It bleeds the region's bands badly — and risks turning a diversion into the open-ground battle that diversions exist to prevent.

costs.resource: real combat strength tied to a position whose whole purpose is to be abandoned
costs.risk: a defense convincing enough to fight over is a defense you may not be able to walk away from

decisionPoints.name: When to Strike the Set
decisionPoints.context: The bands are committing and the lanes are clearing. Somewhere ahead is the moment to fold the deception and run. Too early, and the bands drift back to the lanes before the real traffic is through. Too late, and you are caught on the pan by what you summoned.

options.title: Extract on Schedule
advantages: Pull out at the contracted {DECOY_DAYS} mark no matter what the bands are doing — the traffic window {EMPLOYER} paid for is the only clock that matters
Disciplined and clean: leave before the swarm closes, deception intact, set struck overnight
The lowest-risk exit, if the timing was estimated well
disadvantages: A schedule set before the operation cannot know whether the bands have really committed or are still on the way
Leaving on time but too early lets the nearer bands turn back to the lanes inside the traffic window
If a band is closer than intel believed, 'on schedule' may already be too late
options.consequence: You trust the plan and the clock over the picture in front of you. If the estimate held, the force is gone clean and the lanes stayed empty exactly as long as they needed to. If the bands moved slower or faster than the schedule assumed, the gap between plan and reality costs you either a wasted diversion or a desperate exit.

costs.resource: sticking to a clock set before the enemy's real timing was known
costs.risk: the schedule cannot see the band that is a day ahead of where intel put it

options.title: Hold for Confirmation
advantages: Stay until recon confirms the bands have really committed and the lanes are genuinely clear — leave on the real picture, not the planned one
Guarantees the diversion did its job before you let go of it
Catches a slow band before it can drift back to the lanes
disadvantages: Holding for confirmation means staying on the pan longer, with every extra hour bringing the swarm closer
Word from the lanes travels at courier speed with comms down, so it may arrive after the safe-exit window has closed
You may confirm success and your own encirclement in the same report
options.consequence: You refuse to leave until you know the job is done, and you pay for that certainty in nearness to the threat. It is the surest way to guarantee the lanes stayed clear — and the surest way to still be on the dust plain when the first band tops the dunes {DUNE_RANGE} kilometers out.

costs.resource: extra days on an exposed pan while confirmation crawls in at courier speed
costs.risk: the confirmation that the diversion worked may arrive alongside the band that ends it

options.title: Leave It Running on Timers
advantages: Pull out early but leave the deception running on automation — staged activity, recorded comms chatter, lights on a schedule — so the bands keep racing to an empty stage after you are gone
Your force is clear well before the swarm arrives, yet the lie holds and the lanes stay clear past your departure
The most safety for your force and extra mileage from the deception
disadvantages: An automated deception is fragile — the first band ashore finds an unguarded prize and the curtain drops fast, maybe inside the traffic window
Rigging the set to run itself takes prep time and gear you must then abandon
If the automation fails early, the diversion collapses with no one there to hold it up
options.consequence: You leave the lie to run without you — a stage that performs to an empty house until the audience arrives and finds no one home. It is the safest exit and the most fragile deception. The lanes stay clear as long as no band reaches the compound, and nothing now stands between the bands and the truth but a few timers and the dust.

costs.resource: abandoned automation gear and the sturdiness of the trick, traded for your force's early safety
costs.risk: an unguarded fake collapses the instant the first band walks in, maybe before the traffic is through

entries.event: The show begins. Staged repair activity goes visible on the pan, rumor packets ride outbound couriers, and the dead world starts to look alive to anyone watching the lanes.
First scout contact. A band's recon is spotted on the dune line {DUNE_RANGE} kilometers out, watching. The deception meets its first test: the scouts must see strength, not props.
The bands commit. Lane-watch traffic thins as the first bands leave their posts and move toward the dead world. The diversion is working, and the swarm is forming.
The contracted window closes. {EMPLOYER}'s real traffic should be through the cleared lanes. Your reason to stay has expired — but the bands you summoned are now closest.
Earliest hostile arrival in force. The fastest band reaches attack range of a stage set, and whatever you have not already done about your own extraction, you are doing now under fire.

reactionTimeline.hardDeadline: The traffic window closes at T+{DECOY_DAYS} days, and the swarm arrives close behind it. The two clocks were always going to meet, because a diversion that empties the lanes is a diversion that fills the pan. Your deception force must be gone, or going, before the first band tops the dunes. Stay to admire the work and you become the prize the region's raiders raced each other for, standing on an open plain, defending a building full of fakes.

opforSketch.composition: The region's raider bands, drawn and uncoordinated: {BAND_COUNT}-plus independent groups, each a light-to-medium salvage company (Green to Regular, a Veteran command core in the larger ones), heavy on technicals and fast 'Mechs because raiders prize speed and reach. No band coordinates with another; they race and, if they meet over the prize, fight each other. Heaviest threat is two or more bands arriving close together. Generator should field the bands as separate OPFOR groups on staggered arrivals, with a real chance of band-on-band engagement if the deception holds long enough to make them all converge.
opforSketch.behavior: Greed-driven and impatient: a band that believes a working HPG is in reach abandons lesser raids and races, scouting first and committing hard once it judges a rival might beat it there. They respect apparent strength and will skirmish to test the guard before assaulting. The instant a band confirms the prize is fake, it flips to spite — hunting the tricksters and warning no one, because a humiliated raider keeps his humiliation to himself.

forks.name: OPERATION SILENT LANES
forks.trigger: The deception holds the full window, the force extracts clean, and no band confirms the fake.
forks.consequence: {EMPLOYER}'s traffic is through untouched, and the dead world stays a usable lie. {EMPLOYER} keeps the unit on to run the deception again on a fresh schedule, or to spend the credibility it just built on a bolder second traffic move through lanes the bands still believe are watched by ghosts.

forks.name: OPERATION OPEN STAGE
forks.trigger: The deception is exposed early, or the force is caught on the pan and drawn into a decisive fight.
forks.consequence: The bands learn the HPG was bait and the lanes were the target, and the region's raiders — robbed and humiliated — turn on both your unit and {EMPLOYER}'s real traffic. The next job is a fighting withdrawal off the dead world against bands that now hunt for spite, with the lanes no safer than before.

forks.name: OPERATION ECHO
forks.trigger: The diversion half-works: some bands commit, others stay on the lanes, and the force extracts under pressure.
forks.consequence: The lanes were thinned, not cleared, and {EMPLOYER}'s traffic took losses running them. The next job is a real strike on the one band that did not bite — the disciplined raider still on post — to finish clearing a lane the deception only half-emptied.

storyElementSeed: A tech in a clean coverall walks the dust plain past a row of coolant tanks that ring hollow when grit hits them in the wind. His clipboard is blank. He waves at a dune line fifteen kilometers off, where he is sure someone with good optics is counting how many of him there are.

resourceGates.lackingText: Insufficient funds to stage a major project: the deception runs on cut-rate props and thinner rumor — drop the apparent scale, and accept that the disciplined bands will see through a budget production and stay on the lanes.

No engineering base to rig a self-running set: the automation must be jury-built from field stores — add 4 days of setup and a higher chance the timers fail early and drop the curtain before the traffic is through.

title: OPERATION TOLL ROAD
skeleton: a hunter must dislodge a raider band that has seized a working recharge station and turned it into a tollgate, where the station is the region's only recharge point and must not be destroyed, and the band holds the station's own civilian operators as hostages, so the band must be cleared off a fixed asset intact rather than sunk and the people who run it kept alive
inspiration: Barbary corsair shore-fort tollgates; the hostage-held lighthouse that cannot be shelled
situation:
A JumpShip recharge station is a lighthouse, a tollbooth, and a chokepoint in one fragile structure. Since the Blackout, the {DISTRICT} recharge station is the only one that serves jumps in any direction. Every JumpShip that wants to cross this stretch of the frontier stops there, or it faces a week-long solar charge instead. Four months ago a band that calls itself Coyle's Reckoning took the station. They did not loot it and leave. They are still there, running it.

The Reckoning turned the station into a tollgate. Every ship that recharges has to pay in cargo, fuel, hard currency, or crew. Ships that refuse are turned away to a slow death on solar power, or they are boarded. {EMPLOYER} speaks for the regional shipping firms the toll is bleeding, and reached you through {NPC:employer-contact}. They have been clear about what they want: not a wreck. The station must come out of this working. A destroyed station would not punish the band. It would punish everyone for a generation, because nobody in the Dark Age is building new ones. Treat the intel as fairly solid on the layout but only rough on the band's strength; it is 14 to 35 days old, drawn from toll-victim statements and a station schematic.

The terrain problem is the station itself. It is a Star League-era recharge station: a kilometer of pressurized truss, fuel tanks, the huge sail-furling gear, and a central habitat ring. All of it is irreplaceable, and most of it is deadly to fight inside. A breach near the fuel tanks ends the station. A firefight in the sail gear ends the station's ability to work. The only place a battle can happen without killing the prize is the docking spine and the outer truss. The core is where the band lives and where the hostages are held. It is the place you most need to take, and the place you least dare to fight.

One fact turns this from an assault into a siege. Coyle's Reckoning holds the station's original civilian crew in the core habitat ring: {HOSTAGE_COUNT} operators and their families. They are the only people alive who can keep the station running. The band needs them to work the toll. You need them to deliver a working station. The band knows you must not break the station and must not get the operators killed. The hostages are the band's armor, the station's heart, and the whole point of the contract. They are all in the one compartment nobody can safely storm.

objectives.primary: Clear Coyle's Reckoning off the recharge station and end the toll. Hand it to {EMPLOYER}'s shipping firms whole and still working.
objectives.secondary: Bring the station's civilian operators out alive: {HOSTAGE_COUNT} crew and families. Without them, even an undamaged station is dead, because only they can run it.
objectives.bonus: Take the station before the band can rig it to blow. A station captured with its fuel tanks unmined is worth a permanent garrison contract. A station you had to defuse under fire is a near miss nobody wants to repeat.

complications.name: The Asset That Cannot Break
complications.text: The station is the only recharge point for jumps in any direction, and nobody is building more. Every weapon you fire inside it is aimed at the very thing the contract exists to save.
complications.mechanicalEffect: In the fuel tanks, sail gear, or core habitat, any energy or ballistic shot triggers a roll for catastrophic station damage. Only the docking spine and outer truss allow free fire. If the station is destroyed, the contract fails no matter what happens to the band.

complications.name: The Operators in the Core
complications.text: The civilian crew are held in the core habitat ring. That ring is the band's living quarters and the station's control center. It is the one compartment you cannot storm without killing the very people the contract is meant to save.
complications.mechanicalEffect: The hostages sit in the most fragile compartment, right alongside the band's main strength. Any assault on the core risks killing hostages. Hostage deaths fail the secondary goal, and a working station still needs those people alive. Take the core by some means other than a direct assault, or do not take it at all.

complications.name: The Threat to Scuttle
complications.text: Coyle's Reckoning is not loved, and the band knows it. If cornered, its last piece of leverage is the fuel tanks. Wire them to blow, and your prize and the region's lifeline die together.
complications.mechanicalEffect: Once the band decides the station is lost, a scuttle clock starts and the band begins rigging the fuel tanks. A rigged station must be defused before you can claim it, which turns the job from an assault into bomb disposal against a deadline. To stop the rigging entirely, you must keep the band from ever deciding the station is lost. That takes speed or deception, not pressure.

decisionPoints.name: How to Take the Station
decisionPoints.context: The band sits on a fragile station it will scuttle if cornered, and it holds the only people who can run the place. Every approach carries a cost. Pressure may trigger the scuttle. Patience lets the toll keep bleeding the region. A direct assault risks the hostages. Choose how you go in with all three in mind.

options.title: Storm the Spine, Squeeze the Core
advantages: Take the docking spine and outer truss by force, since that is the one place a fight is safe. Then cut the core off from fuel, air, and escape, and squeeze.
Keeps the shooting away from the fragile compartments and the hostages.
A band cut off on a station it cannot run forever may surrender instead of scuttle.
disadvantages: Squeezing the band pushes it toward the decision that starts the scuttle clock.
Cutting the core's air and power cuts the hostages' air and power too. The squeeze hurts them first.
A siege gives the band time to rig the fuel tanks carefully.
options.consequence: You take the safe ground and tighten the noose. You are betting the band breaks before it decides to take everyone down with it. The fighting stays clean and the station stays whole. But hour by hour, you walk the band toward the exact decision the scuttle clock is waiting for.

costs.resource: The hostages' own air and power, choked off as part of the squeeze on the band they are held with.
costs.risk: A cornered band on a fragile station is one decision away from wiring the fuel tanks.

options.title: Pose as a Paying Ship
advantages: Arrive as a rich merchant willing to pay the toll, dock like any customer, and slip a boarding team into the core before the band knows it is under attack. Surprise instead of siege.
This is the only approach that might take the core before the band ever decides to scuttle.
The hostages and the station are both safest if the band never gets a chance to react.
disadvantages: If the disguise fails at the dock, the fight starts in the worst place, and the surprise belongs to the band, not to you.
A boarding team small enough to pass as a merchant crew is small against a company of raiders.
If the team is spotted before it reaches the core, the band holds both the hostages and the initiative.
options.consequence: You bet everything on getting inside the band's guard before it can reach for its leverage. A clean infiltration takes the core in one stroke, hostages and station and all. A blown one leaves a handful of boarders deep in a hostile station, with the hostages already at the band's mercy and no siege line to fall back on.

costs.resource: The boarding team, sent deep into the station on the strength of a disguise that gets exactly one test.
costs.risk: A disguise blown at the dock hands the band the hostages, the initiative, and your own boarders.

options.title: Turn the Toll Against Them
advantages: Use the band's own greed against it. Arrange a rich-looking 'convoy' of paying ships to pull the band's strength out to the docking spine to collect, which thins the guard on the core.
Lets you pick the time and place of the fight and pull the band off the hostages.
Sets up a core assault against a skeleton guard instead of the band's full weight.
disadvantages: Setting up the bait takes time and willing ships, and the toll keeps running while you prepare.
Drawing the band to the spine is only the setup. The core fight still has to happen fast, before the band rushes back.
If the band smells the trap, it pulls back to the core and digs in around the hostages.
options.consequence: You use the tollgate's own logic to empty the room that matters. Done well, the band's strength is stuck at the far end of a kilometer of truss when you take the core. Done poorly, the band spots its own trick being run against it and pulls together in exactly the place you least want a fight.

costs.resource: The bait convoy and the days to set it up, while the toll keeps bleeding the region.
costs.risk: A band that spots the bait falls back on the hostages and turns the core into a fortress.

decisionPoints.name: The Scuttle Decision
decisionPoints.context: The fight is on, and the band's leader can feel the station slipping away. The fuel tanks are within reach, and the threat to blow them is the band's last card. Decide now how you will handle the moment the band reaches for it.

options.title: Race the Rig
advantages: Drive for the fuel tanks and the core fast enough to take both before the band can finish wiring them. Answer the scuttle threat with pure speed.
Denies the band the time it needs to make the rig real.
If it works, you take the station unmined and secure the bonus.
disadvantages: Racing means pushing hard and fast through the fragile compartments, the exact places where a firefight kills the station.
A half-finished rig you reach too late is still a rig you have to defuse.
Rushing past the hostages puts them at risk in the scramble.
options.consequence: You gamble that you are faster than a frightened band with wire and a deadline. Win the race and the station is whole and clean. Lose it by one compartment and you are defusing bombs in the fuel tanks while the band's rear guard shoots at the people trying to defuse them.

costs.resource: A hard, fast push through the station's most fragile compartments to beat the rig.
costs.risk: A race lost by minutes leaves the station rigged to blow with you standing inside it.

options.title: Offer the Band the Door
advantages: Open a way out. Let the band take its ship and a head start in exchange for the station intact and the hostages alive.
Removes the band's reason to scuttle. A band that can leave has no need to die.
Saves the station, the operators, and your own people in one negotiated stroke.
disadvantages: The band that ran the toll for four months sails away to do it somewhere else, unpunished.
{EMPLOYER}'s shipping firms may have wanted the Reckoning ended, not just moved along.
A band given the door may take the hostages along as travel insurance anyway.
options.consequence: You buy the station and the people with the band's freedom. You meet the letter of the contract cleanly: a working station and live operators.
